title: Why Vishnu keeps coming down
hookLine: Hiranyaksha blocks the way up, and three descents add up to one promise
carry: whenever dharma sinks, vishnu comes down
tomorrow: his brother wants revenge. what boon does he ask for?

cards: Every rescue story has a moment when the hero is almost home and someone steps into the doorway.

Varaha is rising through the waters with the earth on his tusk, and there in the deep is Hiranyaksha, a demon who has been roaming the waters looking for someone strong enough to fight him. He mocks the boar.

teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana, Varaha doesn't drop the earth to answer him.

teach.h: THE EARTH SET DOWN SAFE FIRST.
teach.b: He sets her safely on the water first, and only then turns to fight, and he defeats him.

The Bhagavata gives this demon a surprising past: he and his brother were once Vishnu's own doorkeepers, Jaya and Vijaya, cursed by sages to be born for a time as his enemies. The brother is where the story goes next.
Now step back and look at the three descents together.
A fish, when the Vedas were lost in the flood. A tortoise, when the mountain sank. A boar, when the earth sank.

Each time something holy is going under, and each time Vishnu comes down in the shape that can save it. Hindus have a word for what's going under: dharma, the right order of things, in the world and in a life.

And they have Krishna's words for why he keeps coming, in the Bhagavad Gita. In paraphrase: whenever dharma declines and wrong rises, I come; to protect the good and set things right, I'm born age after age.
That's why the avatars come in a row.
It's one promise, kept in different shapes. And it's why, when a family's world seems to be sinking, many Hindus don't only ask for strength. They pray for Vishnu to come.

how: Pictures of the Dashavatara, Vishnu's ten descents, are a familiar sight in Hindu homes and temples, and Varaha's fight with Hiranyaksha is told right before Narasimha, since the two demons are brothers.

games.q: your cousin asks what a fish, a tortoise and a boar have in common. best answer?
o: each time dharma is sinking, Vishnu comes down in the shape that can save it.
they're three sea gods, each in charge of one creature.
they're Vishnu being punished with animal bodies.
games.why: Krishna says it in the Gita: whenever dharma declines, I come, age after age. fish, tortoise, boar: one promise, three shapes.

practice: Close your eyes and let one of the three descents come back on its own: a fish in the flood, a tortoise under the mountain, a boar in the deep. Stay with whichever one comes, and breathe slowly.
If you pray, ask Vishnu to come down to whatever is sinking in your week; if you don't, simply rest there.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 3.15–3.16 (Jaya and Vijaya, Vishnu's doorkeepers, cursed by the sages to be born as demons)
Bhagavata Purana 3.17–3.19 (Hiranyaksha roams the waters seeking a match; Varaha sets the earth on the water; the fight)
Bhagavad Gita 4.7–4.8 (whenever dharma declines, I come, to protect the good and establish dharma, age after age)
